questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why industry came first to Britain
questions.learningObjective: Explain why Britain's coal endowment mattered for early industry
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks why Britain's coal seams sat close to iron ore and ports, and how that proximity shaped early factory siting

options.text: Proximity reduced fuel and transport costs, letting mills cluster where coal, ore and harbours met
Coal was exported first and iron was imported, so ports mattered most
options.misconception: reverses the direction of early trade flows

options.text: Coal powered steam engines that pumped water from mines and drove mills near raw materials
options.misconception: treats coal as only a heating fuel rather than an energy source

options.text: Government ordered factories to build beside coal seams by law

questions.explanation: Cheap fuel and short hauls lowered costs and encouraged clustering. Coal was not merely export cargo, and siting was market-driven rather than legally mandated.
questions.hint: Think about cost and clustering, not law.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish factory production from the putting-out system
questions.stem: An engineer's brief compares a water-powered mill that gathers workers under one roof with rural households spinning yarn at home

options.text: Both systems use the same machines and the same labour contracts
The mill centralises machinery and supervision while households keep flexible hours and own tools
The putting-out system was always larger and more efficient than mills
options.misconception: assumes rural work outproduced centralised mills

options.text: Mills only appeared after the putting-out system vanished
options.misconception: treats the two systems as strictly sequential

questions.explanation: Centralised mills gathered power, machines and oversight in one place. Rural outwork kept flexible hours and household tools, and the two overlapped rather than replacing each other instantly.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: State the advantage of Watt's separate condenser
questions.stem: An engineer's brief notes that James Watt separated the condenser from the cylinder and asks what problem that solved

options.text: It doubled the speed of the piston by gearing
options.misconception: attributes gains to gearing not thermal efficiency

options.text: It removed the need for any fuel at all
It made the engine run on water instead of steam
It let the cylinder stay hot while steam condensed elsewhere, saving fuel

questions.explanation: Keeping the cylinder hot while condensing steam in a separate vessel cut fuel use. It did not eliminate fuel, change fuel type, or rely on gearing.
questions.hint: Think thermal efficiency, not fuel type.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why early mills followed fast-flowing streams
questions.stem: An engineer's brief places a new textile mill where a stream drops sharply through a narrow valley

options.text: Streams were chosen only because coal was scarce nearby
options.misconception: makes coal scarcity the sole driver

options.text: Fast flow and head give reliable mechanical power before steam engines spread
Narrow valleys prevented workers from leaving the mill
Waterpower was cheaper than labour in all cases

questions.explanation: Head and flow provided mechanical power before steam became practical. Coal scarcity alone did not dictate siting, and waterpower was not always cheaper than labour.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Link enclosure to the supply of wage labour

stimulus.body: Enclosed acres rose while common land shrank, and rural households that had grazed animals on commons lost that supplement. Wages in nearby towns rose modestly as migration increased.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief reads a table showing enclosed acres rising and asks what that implies for factory labour supply

options.text: Common land grew, letting peasants refuse factory work
Enclosure increased farm output so no one needed factory wages
options.misconception: assumes enclosure kept everyone on the land

options.text: Enclosure displaced rural households, swelling the wage-labour pool in towns
Enclosure was irrelevant because workers came from abroad

questions.explanation: Loss of common grazing pushed households toward wage work in towns. Enclosure did not keep everyone farming, and domestic displacement mattered more than immigration.
questions.hint: Follow the land loss to labour supply.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify forms of state support for early industry
questions.stem: An engineer's brief lists tariffs, patents, and turnpike trusts as tools a state used to foster industry

options.text: Support came only from private banks, never government
options.misconception: confuses private finance with public policy

options.text: States only helped by banning imports entirely
The state played no role in early industrialisation
Tariffs, patents and transport investment all lowered risks for industrial ventures

questions.explanation: Tariffs, patents and infrastructure investment all reduced risk. State help was broader than import bans and included public as well as private finance.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Recognise competing explanations for British industrialisation

stimulus.body: One scholar stresses abundant coal and cheap capital; another stresses culture and institutions. Both agree that no single factor suffices and that timing varied by sector.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief weighs two scholarly accounts of why Britain industrialised first

options.text: Only coal mattered, so culture is irrelevant
options.misconception: reduces the debate to one factor

options.text: Scholars disagree on emphasis but agree multiple factors combined
Only institutions mattered, so resources were irrelevant
options.misconception: reduces the debate to the other factor

options.text: The debate is settled and no uncertainty remains

questions.explanation: The accounts differ in emphasis yet both invoke multiple causes. Neither single factor nor settled consensus captures the debate.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Incomes and population in early industrial Britain
questions.learningObjective: Assess claims about living standards during early industrialisation
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks whether rising population in early industrial Britain proves that incomes and living standards rose for workers

answer.exemplar: Rising population alone does not prove rising incomes; it may reflect earlier marriage and cheaper calories, while real wages stagnated for decades before improving later in the nineteenth century.

questions.explanation: Population growth can stem from falling mortality and earlier marriage rather than prosperity. Real wage trends were uneven and often flat until mid-century, so population is an imperfect proxy for living standards.
questions.hint: Population growth is not income growth.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of empire and overseas markets
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks how overseas colonies and Atlantic trade affected demand for British manufactured goods

options.text: Overseas trade had no effect on domestic industry
Colonies produced manufactured goods that competed with Britain
Colonial markets absorbed textiles and hardware, expanding outlets for factory output
Colonies only bought raw cotton, not finished goods
options.misconception: narrows colonial demand to raw materials

questions.explanation: Colonial and Atlantic markets took British textiles and hardware. Colonies were not rival manufacturers, and their demand extended beyond raw cotton.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks why a merchant who once distributed wool to cottages later built a mill with machines inside

options.text: Machines could not be used in cottages at all
options.misconception: overstates technical impossibility of home use

options.text: Cottage workers demanded central mills to escape isolation
options.misconception: attributes the shift to worker preference

options.text: The state forced all production into mills by decree
Centralising machines let the merchant control quality, pace and costs more directly

questions.explanation: Central mills offered direct control over quality, pace and cost. The shift was merchant-driven, not worker-demanded or state-ordered, and some machinery remained usable at home.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how Watt's engine differed from Newcomen's
questions.stem: An engineer's brief compares Watt's engine with Newcomen's and asks what changed in the cycle

options.text: Watt removed the piston and used a turbine instead
Watt kept the cylinder hot and condensed steam separately, cutting waste
Newcomen's engine used no steam at all
Both engines were identical in efficiency

questions.explanation: Watt's separate condenser preserved cylinder heat and reduced waste. He did not remove the piston, Newcomen did use steam, and efficiencies differed markedly.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Recognise limits of waterpower for industrial expansion
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks why mill owners eventually added steam engines beside water wheels

options.text: Steam engines were cheaper to build than water wheels
Waterpower was banned by parliament in 1800
Steam freed siting from river valleys and allowed larger, steadier output
Rivers dried up across Britain in the 1790s

questions.explanation: Steam decoupled mills from rivers and smoothed output. Waterpower was not banned, steam was costlier upfront, and rivers did not dry up.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate enclosure's effects on rural households
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks whether enclosure benefited or harmed the rural poor who lost common grazing rights

answer.exemplar: Enclosure harmed many rural poor by removing grazing and fuel rights that supplemented low wages, pushing some toward factory or seasonal work, though a minority of owners gained consolidated holdings.

questions.explanation: Loss of common rights cut a vital supplement for poor households and pushed many toward wage labour. Gains accrued mainly to larger owners, so effects were sharply unequal.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how patent law encouraged innovation
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks how a patent helped an inventor profit from a new spinning machine

options.text: It banned competitors from ever building similar machines
options.misconception: overstates duration and scope of exclusivity

options.text: It made the invention free for all to use immediately
It guaranteed government purchase of the machine
It granted temporary exclusive rights, letting the inventor license or sell the design

questions.explanation: Patents granted time-limited exclusivity that inventors could license. They did not make designs free, guarantee purchases, or impose permanent bans.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish proto-industrialisation from full industrialisation
questions.stem: An engineer's brief distinguishes rural cottage industry before factories from later factory-based industrialisation

options.text: Proto-industry and factory industry were identical in organisation
Proto-industry expanded rural manufacturing and markets but lacked central power and scale
Proto-industry only existed after steam engines appeared
Factory industry declined into proto-industry over time

questions.explanation: Proto-industry widened rural manufacturing and demand but lacked centralised power and scale. The phases differed in organisation and chronology.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Incomes and population in early industrial Britain
questions.learningObjective: Relate population growth to food supply and prices

stimulus.body: Population rose steadily from 1750 to 1830 while grain prices fluctuated with harvests. Real wages for labourers stayed flat in many decades despite aggregate growth.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief reads a chart of population and grain prices and asks what it shows about workers' welfare

options.text: Grain prices fell steadily, so food was always cheap
Rising population proved every worker became richer
Aggregate growth masked stagnant real wages and volatile food costs for labourers
Real wages doubled for all labourers by 1800

questions.explanation: Aggregate expansion coexisted with flat real wages and volatile grain prices. Population did not ensure prosperity, and prices were not steadily falling.

options.text: Market size mattered only after 1900
A large market reduced the need for any innovation
Home markets only bought imported goods
Broad demand let producers specialise and spread fixed costs over many units

questions.explanation: Large demand enabled specialisation and cost spreading. It did not remove incentives to innovate, and domestic consumers did buy home manufactures.

Factories imposed fixed hours and punctuality, replacing task-oriented rural rhythms
Clocks were used only to measure output, not time
Rural workers refused all time discipline forever

questions.explanation: Factories fixed hours and demanded punctuality, unlike task-oriented cottage work. Rural workers were not already clock-bound, and resistance was partial.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the sun-and-planet gear
questions.stem: An engineer's brief asks how Watt's engine converted reciprocating motion into rotary motion for mills

options.text: Steam pressure rotated the cylinder housing
The condenser itself spun the shaft directly
Sun-and-planet gearing turned the piston's back-and-forth motion into rotation
No conversion was needed because pistons already rotated

questions.explanation: Sun-and-planet gearing converted reciprocating piston motion into rotary shaft motion. The condenser did not drive rotation, and pistons do not rotate.

The pond was mainly for washing raw cotton
Sluices increased the river's total water volume
Storing water smoothed power output across dry spells and seasons

questions.explanation: Ponds stored water to smooth power through dry periods. They were not for washing cotton, did not create water, and were functional not decorative.

Consolidated fields and selective breeding raised yields even as smallholders lost access
Only crop rotation changed; field size was irrelevant
Displacement never affected labour supply

questions.explanation: Consolidation and improved breeding raised yields while smallholders lost access. Yields did not fall, and field size did matter for the labour pool.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief applies Malthusian logic to a period when population grew faster than food supply

Food supply never affects wages in any era
Malthus argued population growth was impossible

questions.explanation: Malthusian pressure can depress real wages when population outruns food. He did not predict automatic wage rises, and food supply does affect wages.

Skilled artisans could adapt and improve machines, bridging craft and factory methods
Artisans worked only in agriculture

questions.explanation: Skilled artisans adapted and improved machinery. They did not block all innovation, and unskilled labour alone did not drive technical change.

questions.explanation: Low power needs and flexible labour suited dispersed work. Cottage work was not always more profitable, and those goods did not need giant engines.

Repeated heating and cooling of the cylinder wasted energy, which separation avoided
Fuel savings came from using less water, not less coal
The cylinder was cooled to freeze the steam

questions.explanation: Repeated heating and cooling of the cylinder wasted fuel; separation avoided that. The condenser did not create steam, and coal not water was saved.

Rivers always froze in summer

questions.explanation: Low summer flow cut available power. Wheels did not melt, and stops were hydrological not behavioural.

questions.explanation: Watt's early engine pumped water from mines. Rotary mill drive came later, and ship or electrical uses were anachronistic.

questions.subject: EUROPEAN_HISTORY
questions.topic: Incomes and population in early industrial Britain
questions.learningObjective: Explain how urbanisation affected mortality and health

stimulus.body: Urban populations grew rapidly while death rates in towns exceeded those in rural areas. Crowded housing and contaminated water accompanied early industrial expansion.

questions.stem: An engineer's brief reads a table of urban death rates and asks what it implies about industrial growth

options.text: Urban growth had no health effects at all
Towns were always healthier than the countryside
Death rates fell to zero in industrial towns
Rapid urbanisation brought health costs that offset some gains from higher wages

questions.explanation: Urban growth carried health costs that offset wage gains. Towns were less healthy, death rates did not vanish, and health effects were real.

Colonies refused to export raw materials
